title: Janhvi Kapoor Takes Indian Muslin to Paris Fashion Week Gala
excerpt: At the BoF 500 Gala in Paris, the actor wore a custom Pankaj S Heritage ivory ensemble in 460-count Bengal muslin — khud-rang, woven in India — with jewellery-like embellished sleeves.
body:
• Janhvi Kapoor attended the Business of Fashion BoF 500 Gala in Paris on October 3 wearing a custom Pankaj S Heritage ivory ensemble, styled by Rhea Kapoor.
  • The centrepiece was a 460-count Bengal muslin saree — khud-rang, meaning unbleached — woven in India and historically described as fine as air.
  • Instead of a necklace, Kapoor wore jewellery as sleeves: polkis, garnets, emeralds, Saraafa tassels, and kiran-and-resham fringing extending toward the wrists.
  • It was her second Paris Fashion Week appearance of the season after the Miu Miu show, following her Cannes saree debut earlier in the year.

The look

Janhvi Kapoor brought Indian textile craft onto one of fashion's biggest stages this week. At the Business of Fashion BoF 500 Gala in Paris on October 3, the 29-year-old actor wore a custom ivory ensemble by Pankaj S Heritage, styled by her cousin Rhea Kapoor, during Paris Fashion Week.

https://x.com/HiFiTalkies/status/2106702226458898896

The outfit reworked the six-yard saree rather than repeating it. The drape sat low-slung with a fallen pallu and bare shoulders, giving the traditional form a sculptural, contemporary line, according to reports from Hindustan Times and t2Online.

But the fabric did the real talking. The saree was cut from 460-count Bengal muslin — muslin khadi — woven entirely in India. Stylist Rhea Kapoor described the textile as khud-rang, or unbleached, and "woven like air," noting it is also known as baft-e-hawa, shabnami, or chandani.

"Woven like air — baft-e-hawa, shabnami or chandani. The truest form of luxury: muslin khadi, woven solely in India."

— Rhea Kapoor, celebrity stylist

Context & background

The annual BoF 500 Gala gathers designers, models, executives, and entrepreneurs shaping the fashion industry, and Kapoor was among the Indian names on the guest list this year. The event was her second Paris Fashion Week appearance after the Miu Miu fashion show, per t2Online.

Kapoor has been building a record of taking the saree international. Earlier, she made her case for the six-yard drape at Cannes in a wet-look, crinkled white chiffon saree by London label Di Petsa, also styled by Rhea Kapoor. The Paris look pushes the same idea further — swapping the French Riviera's sultry styling for heritage craft as the headline.

The details

The ivory muslin kept the palette deliberately quiet so the embellishments could carry the drama. The blouse took a sculpted bralette silhouette with intricate ruching — a corset-inspired construction that stayed fluid with the drape, per Hindustan Times.

The sleeves were the showstopper. Designed to read as jewellery rather than fabric, they were set with polkis, garnets, and emeralds, combined with traditional Saraafa tassels and kiran-and-resham fringing. The jewellery story continued off the garment: a multi-layered wristpiece with hanging tassels echoed the sleeves, finished with vintage-inspired gold studs and a statement cocktail ring.

Her beauty look was pared back on purpose. A sleek low bun kept the neck and shoulders bare, with warm-toned makeup, defined brows, a sharp winged eye, and a matte nude lip — polished without competing with the couture.

Diaspora angle

For diaspora audiences, this is the fashion story that keeps giving. Every major Western red carpet where an Indian star arrives in a saree — and in a fabric woven on Indian looms, no less — makes the drape easier to wear with confidence anywhere from London to New Jersey. The 460-count muslin detail matters too: it puts the spotlight on the weavers and karigars behind the glamour, a craft economy many diaspora families have personal ties to.

What's next

Kapoor remains one to watch on the international fashion circuit, and the Rhea Kapoor styling partnership shows no sign of cooling. The larger question is whether Indian textile heritage — muslin, chikankari, handloom — keeps moving from costume-drama context into contemporary red-carpet design. On the evidence of October 3, the momentum is on the weavers' side.
